Area.evidence_source: Collectively, our case studies support the work of Burns (1980), Pacht (1984), and Blatt (1995) and are consistent with other literature which emphasizes the complex and most destructive elements of the relationship between perfectionism and suicide. In the first of our case studies, Ryan's striving for perfection drove him to the point of agony and eventually despair. In the second, Sam's self-criticism and self-doubt, together with unrealistically ideal expectations and dichotomous thinking, made for a devastating combination. For Dan, who was also highly self-critical and terrified of failure, the reality of failure was finally too much to bear. Perfectionism predisposed all three of these individuals to anxiety and depression. In all three we catch sight of the psychological turmoil affected by a uniquely untenable position: the setting of exceptionally high standards and hopes but with no room for alternatives presents a no-win scenario because that perfection is nonexistent. People with such high personal standards and perfectionistic expectations are therefore likely to experience more punishment than reward in life (Burns, 1980) and are likely to end up frustrated. Thus, there is nothing wrong with having high standards and expectations, but when perfectionistic thinking is accompanied by excessive self-criticism and self-doubt, obsessive fear of failure, the inability to enjoy achievements, and the type of "all or nothing" thinking where anything other than complete success is perceived to be equivalent to total failure, the components for potential catastrophe may be at hand. While explanations for suicides are always complex, and for some cases the relative contribution of perfectionism will vary, this article has focused on the extreme potency that certain profiles of perfectionism can claim in the path to suicide. Our analyses provide important insights into the efficacy of existing theories and the destructive forces that lead some talented but exceptionally self-critical and perfectionistic young people to take their own lives.
